name: durable-subscriber
intent: Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available.
problem: A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.
context: Broker-mediated publish-subscribe messaging where consumers are intermittently offline but individual messages matter: JMS topics, MQTT sessions, Kafka consumer groups, NATS JetStream durable consumers, cloud topic subscriptions. It presumes the messaging system can store messages (or positions) durably, so it is as much a broker-configuration decision as a client one, and it presumes at-least-once delivery is acceptable once the consumer is idempotent. It does not apply to in-process notification or to broadcast where only the newest value counts.
benefits: No gap loss: messages published while the consumer is down are delivered after reconnection, without the publisher knowing or caring that the consumer was away.
The subscription identity is explicit and survives process restarts and redeployments (subscription name plus client id, consumer group, durable consumer name, MQTT client id).
Catch-up is automatic and ordered: the broker replays the retained backlog, or the consumer resumes from its committed position, so recovery needs no bespoke backfill job.
Deployment freedom: the consumer can be scaled down, upgraded or moved without a coordinated drain-first procedure.
The backlog is observable: retained depth or consumer lag becomes a first-class operational metric for the downstream system.
Retention is a policy knob rather than a surprise: capacity and cost are bounded by message expiry, queue or offset quotas, or session expiry.
tradeoffs: Retention is finite and quietly asymmetric to the pattern's promise: a subscriber offline longer than the retention limit (message expiry, offset retention, session expiry) loses its place, and resuming at 'latest' skips exactly the backlog the pattern exists to preserve.

Backlogs accumulate when nobody drains them: an abandoned or slow subscription consumes broker storage and memory, and a long outage turns into a replay burst that can overwhelm the returning consumer.
Durable is not exactly-once: redelivery is the normal outcome of a crash between processing and acknowledgement, so the consumer must be idempotent and own deduplication.

The operational surface grows: subscription lifecycle (create, verify, expire, delete), broker persistence (often off or short by default) and per-subscription access control all become part of the deployment.
Ordering guarantees hold at most per subscription or per partition; rebalances, session loss and parallel consumers reorder or redistribute the catch-up.

Stored backlogs widen the data footprint: sensitive payloads reside in the broker for the whole retention period, so broker encryption and access control now cover message history, not just transport.

participants.responsibility: Publishes messages to the pub-sub channel without knowing which subscribers are connected or how much backlog any of them owes.
Carries the published messages and owns the topic/subscription namespace in which durability is declared.
The named, persisted subscription record (subscription name plus client id, consumer group, durable consumer name, MQTT session) that identifies the subscriber across restarts and owns its backlog.
Holds the undelivered messages - or the subscriber's committed position plus the retained log/queue - for the offline subscriber, bounded by the retention policy.
The consumer application or endpoint that re-attaches with the same subscription identity, drains the retained backlog and then resumes normal consumption.

Bounds replay (batch size, rate, idle/backoff) and defines when progress is durable (acknowledge or commit only after the side effect), turning the backlog into an at-least-once stream the consumer can survive.

use_cases: A Kafka-backed order-processing service that is redeployed or scaled to zero while events keep arriving: the consumer group resumes from its committed offsets and replays what it missed.
An IoT or mobile client on an intermittent link: an MQTT persistent session holds QoS 1/2 publications for its client id and delivers them when the client reconnects.

A partner integration that receives published documents while the partner's system is down: an unshared JMS durable subscription, or a cloud topic subscription, is registered on their behalf and holds the backlog until they acknowledge it.
A nightly audit or analytics consumer that must see every published change: the day's backlog is drained in bounded batches and acknowledged as it is persisted.
A ledger or compliance consumer that must never silently skip events: retention and lag alarms are configured so an offline subscriber is noticed before its backlog expires.

A cloud event-driven architecture (SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO): SNS preserves ordering and deduplication while SQS queues hold messages for durable fan-out to Lambda or EC2 consumers, with DLQs capturing failed deliveries for replay.

An industrial SCADA/IoT sensor fleet where devices connect sporadically over unstable networks: MQTT persistent sessions with a long session expiry interval preserve every telemetry reading until each device reconnects, even after multi-day outages.

A financial audit trail that must immutably record every state-changing event: events are durably retained in Kafka or JetStream and consumed by a compliance subscriber that must not skip or duplicate entries; idempotent deduplication and offset commits after durable persistence enforce this.

A supply-chain or logistics event-sourcing system where downstream services reconstruct state by replaying events after a crash or deliberate seek: the durable consumer starts from the committed position and replays the missing event window atomically with the state reconstruction.

A cross-region disaster-recovery subscriber that mirrors events to a secondary site: the durable subscription in the secondary region receives every event from the primary's topic, with a DLQ holding any events that fail cross-region delivery for manual retry.

A JMS topic consumer that must receive publications made while it is offline: the client reconnects with the same client identifier and durable subscription name, and the provider retains messages until acknowledgement, expiry, or unsubscribe.

An MQTT 3.1.1 device gateway that reconnects with the same client identifier and CleanSession=0: the broker resumes the stored session and queues matching QoS 1/2 publications for delivery after the link returns.

A NATS JetStream billing worker that restarts after an outage: it binds to the same durable consumer name and explicit-acks each message, so the server resumes its acknowledgement floor and redelivers unacknowledged work.

An Azure Service Bus fan-out topology: topic subscriptions are durable by default and each subscription stores its own copy of matching messages, so a receiver that reconnects later still drains its backlog; client-affine durable subscriptions bind the durable state to a stable client id.

A high-throughput replay consumer on RabbitMQ Streams: the consumer attaches with a stable tracking reference (name) and periodically stores its offset server-side, so a restart resumes from the last stored offset instead of re-reading the whole stream.

An event-sourced system on Google Cloud Pub/Sub that must reprocess history after a bug fix: the subscription enables acknowledged-message retention (default window 7 days, up to 31) and is seeked back to a past timestamp or snapshot to replay already-acked messages.
avoid_when: The subscriber is always online and only needs fan-out: a plain non-durable publish-subscribe subscription, or an in-process Observer/Event Aggregator, is enough.
Only the latest state matters (sensor readings, presence, prices): keep a retained or last-value record, or read current state from the system of record instead of replaying history.
The consumer can reconstruct anything it missed from the source of truth: rebuild by querying rather than retaining a backlog for it.
Retention cannot be afforded and downstream loss is acceptable (high-volume telemetry that is sampled anyway): stay non-durable and monitor, instead of pretending to guarantee delivery.
The messages are work items for exactly one consumer: this is a point-to-point concern; use a single-consumer queue with competing consumers.
anti_patterns: "Durable subscription as exactly-once": assuming the broker's retention removes the need for an idempotent receiver, then double-posting after every crash redelivery.
"Create and forget": subscribing once and never expiring or deleting the subscription, so decommissioned subscribers keep accumulating broker storage indefinitely.
"Unbounded catch-up": replaying the whole backlog synchronously at full speed on restart, turning a subscription into a self-inflicted outage.
"Accidental non-durability": deploying with clean sessions, generated client ids, ephemeral consumer names or auto.offset.reset=latest while believing the backlog is being retained.
"Durable everything": making ephemeral high-volume streams durable for every subscriber, paying storage and replay cost for messages nobody will read.
"Slow-consumer overflow": not bounding pending-message limits so a slow consumer silently drops messages instead of back-pressuring or alerting.
"Persistence mismatch": using DURSUB=YES (subscription durable) with non-persistent messages, so the subscription survives but in-flight messages are lost on broker restart.
"Identity conflict": running multiple logical consumers with the same durable subscription name or client ID, causing the broker to merge or fight over the shared backlog.
"Untested cutover": promoting a new deployment without verifying that the subscription is recreated correctly and backlog continuity is preserved after maintenance or failover.
design_principles: Temporal decoupling: producer and consumer availability are independent, and the broker owns the gap between them.
Explicit, stable identity: a durable subscription exists only through a name the consumer can reuse (subscription name plus client id, consumer group, durable consumer name).
Bounded retention as declared policy: every backlog bound states how long an outage may last before the data is declared lost.
At-least-once delivery completed by the consumer: idempotence and deduplication are part of the pattern's contract, not an optimization.
Lifecycle ownership with least privilege: the backlog is stored data with an owner who must create, observe and eventually delete the subscription.
best_practices: Declare the subscription identity (name, client id, group id, durable consumer name) in deployment configuration and keep it stable across releases.
Set retention explicitly — message expiry, queue or offset quota, offset retention, session expiry — from the longest outage you are willing to survive, and alarm before it is reached.
Drain the backlog in bounded batches and acknowledge or commit only after the side effect is durable, using the same discipline during catch-up as during normal operation.
Make handlers idempotent and deduplicate on a message identity, because redelivery is the expected outcome of a crash.
Monitor backlog depth or consumer lag per subscription; alert on sustained growth and on the age of an offline subscription.
Give every subscription a lifecycle: create it declaratively, verify it exists in production, and delete it when the subscriber is retired.
Verify that the broker's persistence is actually enabled (several brokers default to in-memory storage) before promising durability.
Use CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE or transacted sessions for critical subscriptions; AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE may acknowledge before the side effect is durable, silently losing messages on crash.
Pair persistent sessions with QoS 1 or QoS 2 for offline delivery; QoS 0 messages are not reliably queued for offline clients.
Set a bounded pending-message limit (max_ack_pending, MAXDEPTH, memory queue cap) aligned with handler latency and peak rate to prevent silent message drops on slow consumers.
Configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for failed deliveries so poison messages are preserved and can be retried or audited instead of discarded.
Align the session expiry or retention period with business tolerance for stale data and storage budget; indefinite retention costs more and widens the data footprint.
For Kafka: prefer cooperative-sticky rebalancing (Kafka 2.4+) to minimise pause duration during deployments and avoid stop-the-world rebalances.
For NATS JetStream: use the consume pattern for high-throughput continuous workers; use fetch for batch jobs with controlled processing rounds, and set expires to bound latency on quiet streams.
For MQTT: always re-read the session-present flag on reconnect; if the broker reports no session present, re-subscribe to avoid silent subscription gaps.
For IBM MQ (DURSUB=YES): pair with DEFPSIST=YES on the DEST and persistent publishers so in-flight messages survive a queue-manager restart, not just the subscription definition.

For JMS: a durable subscription can have only one active subscriber at a time; a new subscriber attaching with the same identity resumes the previous state — coordinate identity management to prevent accidental takeover.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) — Durable Subscriber (Messaging Endpoints chapter).
